title: Over 4 Million Americans Dropped From SNAP as Sweeping Food Aid Overhaul Takes Hold
excerpt: A rapid decline in food stamp participation since last July has left millions without grocery assistance, with children and immigrants bearing the brunt of tightened eligibility rules.
body:
• SNAP enrollment has fallen by over 4 million — a 10% drop — since President Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill in July 2025, with about 1 million fewer children receiving benefits across 19 states
  • The law expanded work requirements to ages 55–64, ended eligibility for refugees and asylum seekers without green cards, and imposed stricter documentation rules that advocates say are overwhelming state systems
  • Arizona has seen the steepest decline, with enrollment nearly halving, while a bipartisan group of over 200 mayors has urged Congress to reverse or delay the changes

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — the federal safety net that helped more than 42 million Americans buy groceries — has shed over 4 million participants in under a year, according to Agriculture Department data analyzed by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. The sharp decline followed President Donald Trump's signing of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, 2025, which cut projected SNAP spending by $187 billion over a decade.

Many of those dropped are children. In 19 states that provided age-disaggregated data, about 1 million fewer children are now receiving federal food aid compared to July 2025, according to NPR.

What Changed

The legislation rewrote core eligibility rules. Work requirements, previously capped at age 55, now extend to 64. The exemption for parents caring for children was narrowed from those with kids under 18 to those with children 14 and younger. States can no longer waive work rules for homeless recipients or those in high-unemployment areas.

Documentation demands have also intensified. In Kansas, recipients must fill out a 30-page application with 200 questions for benefits averaging about $150 per month, according to advocacy group Appleseed Center for Law and Justice.

"People are already jumping through hoops to get the food that they need. Any more restrictions or requirements on the program really do create hardships."

— Haley Kottler, Appleseed Center for Law and Justice

The law also ended SNAP eligibility for refugees, asylum seekers, and human trafficking survivors who have not yet obtained a green card — a process that takes at least a year and often longer due to processing delays. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that as many as 90,000 people could lose eligibility in an average month because of this provision alone.

The Numbers, State by State

Nearly every state has seen declines, ranging from a few thousand in New Hampshire to roughly half a million in Texas. Arizona recorded the steepest drop: enrollment fell from 892,565 in July 2025 to 448,976 by February 2026 — a decline of nearly 50%, according to USDA data reported by USA Today.

Milt Liu, president of St. Mary's Food Bank in Arizona, told NPR his organization is distributing more food than ever. "It's not just because people are losing their benefits," Liu said, noting that rising costs of groceries, gas, and housing are compounding the pressure.

The New York Federal Reserve Bank recently reported "a remarkable increase in food insecurity, particularly among lower- and middle-income households and households with young children."

A Divided Response

The White House has framed the decline as a success. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins called the changes "a celebration of work and the dignity of work," citing 900 arrests for SNAP fraud and $132 million in recovered funds. At a House Agriculture Committee hearing in June, Republican lawmakers pointed to 450,000 cases of false Social Security numbers and nearly 200,000 cases of benefits paid to dead recipients.

"They haven't been moved off of SNAP. They've been kicked off of SNAP. We all should be ashamed of that."

— Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Massachusetts

On the other side, a bipartisan group of over 200 mayors sent a letter to the Senate Agriculture Committee in late July asking lawmakers to reverse or delay some of the cuts. Democratic lawmakers and food security advocates describe the situation as "incredibly alarming."

More Changes Ahead

The belt-tightening isn't over. Starting October 1, 2026, states must cover 75% of SNAP administrative costs, up from 50%. By October 2027, most states will also be required to pay up to 15% of food benefits the federal government currently covers, based on error rates. For New York alone, that could mean $1.2 billion in additional costs.

Advocates worry these financial pressures will push states to further restrict access or reduce benefits.

Impact on Immigrant Communities

The changes carry particular weight for immigrant communities, including South Asian families navigating the U.S. immigration system. The law's elimination of SNAP eligibility for refugees and asylum seekers until they obtain permanent residency creates a gap that can last years. Indian families arriving through humanitarian channels or sponsorship pathways face the same waiting period, and advocates report a broader chilling effect — many eligible immigrants are avoiding the program over fears that using benefits could affect their immigration status under the proposed public charge rule.

"Taking away their food stamp access during their first year in the United States is really pulling the rug out from under their ability to find their footing," Julia Gelatt of the Migration Policy Institute told Harvest Public Media.
nri_angle: The law's elimination of SNAP eligibility for refugees and asylum seekers until they obtain green cards directly affects South Asian immigrant families, while the proposed public charge rule creates a chilling effect discouraging eligible immigrants from accessing benefits.
